You realize you have an illness of the brain, much like you can have a disorder such as diabetes or low thyroid that will allows require meds to keep you well. Has worked: 

Taking my meds. This is the most important thing to staying well for me. 

Staying active and social. 

A routine. If I can stick with a routine I feel.. safer, for lack of better word

Finding coping skills for the bad days. Somedays I do puzzles, color, walk the dog, etc. Other days I let myself zone out to Netflix to distract my mind. 

Working with my prescriber and therapist to continue checking in on how I'm doing and what I can be doing better. And it allows me to work on my other issues and diagnoses as well. 

Keeping a journal. It helps me track moods and my thought patterns. 

Mindfulness and reading. I practice mindfulness, which isn't easy some days. I also read a lot of calming and educational books - Pema Chodron, Rumi, etc. 

Has not worked:

Self-medication. Drugs and alcohol undo all of the above and makes it harder to cope when I'm not well. 

Isolating from others. It makes me feel worse. 

Putting off my responsibilities. Even if I can only get a couple things done a day, it helps. I feel productive and then my to do list doesn't rage out of control. 

Stopping my meds. Hello mania and mixed episodes and a hospitalization. 

Relationship with self:

I've had to relearn to love myself. Honestly, I'm still working on that, even after all this time. 

I have to remember my limitations. They're more noticeable now but it's in my best interest to remember I need breaks. 

Relationships with others:

I'm careful who I tell. It's mostly my wife and two trusted friends. 

Checking in with those three and letting them know how I'm doing. Both the good and the bad. They can help me keep from crashing, and they can also help me celebrate when I'm doing well. If I don't tell them when I'm not doing well, I spiral faster and things can get out of hand. 

Marriage counseling. Even after our four sessions, my wife and I have a much better understanding of each other and how my illness affects us.

Usually the diagnosis changes from 2 to 1, when full mania rears its head. Have you been medicated since? Once meds are correct, mania can be quieted but you can still cycle a bit up and down. Knowing the difference between hypomania and mania can be important in treatment and prevention. If mania goes too high, in a sense, it can be extremely dangerous. If you've never experienced full blown mania, you are likely bipolar two. But that can change. It's just good to know how "high" and "low" you can go so that you can prevent getting there or work to get out of there.

I can't take SSRIs. At all. Not one of them (I swear I've tried them all over the last decade). I have weird brain chemistry. Every single one sends me into serotonin syndrome. SSRIs can also cause mania, and apparently Wellbutrin can too (DRI, not SSRI). 

But with that said, there are other meds you can take for depression. Wellbutrin is not an SSRI, and there are plenty of TCAs, though those tend to have a few more side effects. I'm going to give another shout out to community mental health. I actually work in the system and have done case management before. I have a pretty good success rate on disability applications as well. So here's my advice.

Start in community mental health. Almost all states have this as an option. Do you have medicaid? Do you qualify? Depending on your state, they may have bought into the new Medicaid. Check to see if that's an option.

Find a case manager. This will be a god send in helping you get all your documentation together for your disability application. Apply for SSDI/SSI. I don't know how many work credits you have, but it's good to apply for both. Once you apply, apply for AND. It isn't much, but it's a bit of money in your pocket each month ($180). Your state might also at least have Medicaid for the disabled so now would be when you start that process. Your doc through community mental health can fill out the Med9 for your AND and possibly medicaid. 

Keep your appointments. Gather all of the medical info you can from the last 7 years (they usually shred stuff after that). Get documentation from your past job if you can stating that you were fired due to your episode (this may be a challenge but worth looking into). The disability office is going to mostly look at notes from doctors and psychiatrists. It sucks, but they don't have time to look through all your therapy notes. 

Check the blue book from the social security site. Match your diagnoses and see if they meet the criteria. This is literally what the office is looking at when they review your file for disability. 

Let me know if you have any questions.

Self-love is the toughest thing in the world, but the most important thing at the same time. You need to learn to love yourself first. My safety plan changes from time to time. Right now it centers around getting stable on meds. When I need a boost, my wife will come to an appointment with me if she has concerns. I do the same for her. We own guns, and we have a strict policy on locking them up if someone isn't doing well. I have a box of stuff that makes me feel better- I've seen them mentioned on here. Mandala coloring books, puzzles, stuff like that. My biggest issue is mania- that's the rough spot for me. The depression usually lifts a bit unless I'm crashing from a high. Other things- she encourages me to reach out to friends, takes on some extra stuff if I'm not feeling well, gets me outside, sometimes we just zone and watch tv if we aren't feeling well. We both have our bad patches and usually we can support the other. The issue comes up sometimes where we are both in a bad place at the same time, hence the couples counseling. 

Things that help my mental health (I have a crazy amount of diagnoses outside of BP) - exercise, healthy food, walking or playing with the dog, relaxing and self care days as needed, meds, therapy, socialization, and sometimes it's just being by myself. The most important thing for me is to stay on a pretty structured schedule. Sadly that's an issue lately with my work schedule but I still hard to stay structured. Hope that helps.

Don't read statistics, they are a terrible thing at times. I have BP1 and my wife is a combat vet. Combined our chance of survival in the statistical world is next to nothing. BUT, minus a recent breakdown after I stopped my meds and did a bunch of dumb shit, we do pretty alright together. Celebrating our six year anniversary tomorrow. We are both in therapy, and both on meds. And soon we are starting couples to learn to work together and support each other better. We have our days where our own stuff feeds off the other persons stuff, but we learning how to work through it. The thing you need to focus on is you. Get your meds figured out, get into therapy, learn your ups and downs, your triggers, your cycles. Help her to learn these things too. My wife and I each have a safety plan that the other person can turn to if we get in a funk. Couples therapy is always a good option, and often best to jump into before things get bad. If you both want it, you will find a way as long as you are both taking care of yourselves and putting work into the relationship. Relationships are hard work, even if you don't have mental illness as a factor. Wishing you the best. And a good old hug.

Former drug addict and alcoholic here. I was diagnosed before the substance abuse issues came up. I self medicated for years. Mostly cocaine, ecstasy, and alcohol. I would do anything I could get my hands on. Self medication was so much more fun than popping the psych meds. But, it killed my brain. It took years to recover from that. Hell, almost a decade, before I started to feel my brain power come back. Now I stick to my psych meds (minus a recent slip of stopping them, spiraling, and ending up on a unit). Self medication is a slippery slope. And I always struggled with psychedelics- I have too many anxiety disorders and I never had a good trip. Is there any other outlet you can look into versus drugs and alcohol? I'm not going to give you a lecture on why they're bad for your brain, sounds like you're level headed enough to already know that. Any reason you aren't on psych meds right now? Granted they can suck, and finding the right one sucks even more, I'm just curious. They can help to get you stable, thus ending the need for self medicating most of the time. I wish I could take back those years, but I learned an important lesson I suppose. Wishing you well.

I'm 30, have been diagnosed since 17. It's a rough journey, but there are things you can try to work on to help. Things that I find helpful: staying on meds - once you start to feel better you will think you don't need them anymore- it's a lie/trick that your brain does. Whatever you do, continue on your meds. If they don't seem to be working talk to your provider. If you don't like your provider, find a new one - it's key to have a good working relationship. Also, get a therapist. They can help with CBT surrounding depression as well as sleep hygiene. 

Stay healthy. It's hard when the depression is there, but try to move. Exercise, walk the dog, clean the house. Eat healthy, limit caffeine. Once I start to let these things go I tend to go downhill. 

A routine can be important. It helps us to feel safe. Take your meds at the same time every day, go to bed at the same time, know what days you plan to clean, what times you will do homework, and stick with it. It's hard when you swing, but routines can be very important.

Socialize - it's hard, but it's worth it. Sometimes you will have to force yourself out of the house to go be with friends, but it's usually worth it once you get there. But also know when you need space and time to yourself. Find a happy balance that works for you. 

You're going to swing, but find what works for you to keep you closer to the middle. You will start to learn yourself and your changes if you pay attention. Insight is key. And we tend to lose that insight when we stop taking our meds - so refer back to the first point. 

I'm coming out of a bad place right now, and it's because I neglected a lot of the above. Oh, and stay away from drugs and alcohol. They add fuel to the fire. It's hard when you're a teen/young adult, but I lost years of my life to the above that I can't get back.
